The facility was modified to accommodate an inlet flow angle variation of around 95° from the original minimum of 33.8° to the maximum of 78.6°.
Midspan exit total pressure and flow angle measurements were obtained at seven inlet flow angles, with five flow conditions for each inlet angle.
The inlet Reynolds numbers varied from 6.83×10^5 to 0.85×10^5, and two isentropic exit Mach numbers of 0.74 and 0.34 were tested.

At negative incidence angles, the non-uniform exit static pressures indicated a converging exhaust section created by the blade row and back wall, which accelerated the flow and resulted in a negative pressure gradient.
As the incidence angle decreased from positive to negative values, the exit flow angle became more negative, and the total pressure loss increased, especially at the lower Reynolds number conditions.
The blade loading became more favorable (higher suction side pressures) at negative incidence angles, and the loading decreased with decreasing Reynolds number.
The losses decreased with negative incidence and increased with decreasing Reynolds number, while the exit flow angles became more negative with decreasing incidence angle.
The loss levels decreased as the Zweifel coefficient increased, indicating a more optimized blade loading at higher Zweifel coefficients.
The study supports the development of variable-speed power turbine (VSPT) technology for the NASA Large Civil Tilt Rotor (LCTR) vehicle, which requires a wide range of blade incidence angles.

The facility modifications and the generated dataset provide a valuable resource for CFD code validation, particularly for cases with extreme incidence angle variations and transitional Reynolds number conditions.
The study demonstrates the importance of understanding the effects of incidence angle and Reynolds number variations on the aerodynamic performance of turbine blade sets.
The research aims to improve the design and performance of variable-speed power turbines for advanced aircraft applications.
The transonic turbine cascade facility has been used in previous studies to acquire detailed aerodynamic and heat transfer measurements for CFD code validation.
The current study supports the development of VSPT speed-change technology for the NASA LCTR vehicle, which operates over a nearly 50% speed range from takeoff to altitude cruise.

The cascade facility has the ability to operate over a wide range of Reynolds numbers and Mach numbers, which is crucial for investigating the performance of turbine blade sets under various operating conditions.
